Hosen
HOH-zen
noun (plural)
The old plural of hose, from the Saxon hosa — a covering for the legs, and by extension breeches or trousers. The form hosen is the older plural, as oxen to ox.

Biblical Definition

Hosen occurs once, and the verse is a masterpiece of deliberate detail: “Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace” (Dan 3:21). Why does the Holy Ghost trouble to itemise the wardrobe of three men about to be burned? Because of what is said thirty verses later, when the princes and governors gather to inspect them: the fire had no power upon their bodies, “nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them” (Dan 3:27). The clothing is listed going in so that it may be checked coming out. Even the smell was absent. Only one thing burned in that furnace, and Nebuchadnezzar himself reports it: “Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt” (Dan 3:25) — they went in bound, and the ropes were all that the flames consumed. Note also the ground of their courage, spoken before the deliverance and not after: our God is able to deliver us, but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods. Their obedience did not depend on the outcome, which is why it is worth imitating.

Webster 1828 Definition

The old plural of hose: coverings for the legs, breeches. Itemised among the garments of the three Hebrews cast into the furnace, so that their preservation might be verified.

HOSE, n. A covering for the legs; stockings; breeches.

HOSEN, the old plural, as oxen from ox.

From the Saxon hosa; German Hose, breeches.

Dan 3:21 lists coats, hosen, hats, and other garments.

Dan 3:27 verifies that not one of them was changed, nor the smell of fire upon them.

Key Scripture

Dan 3:17 — "If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king."

Dan 3:21 — "Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen , and their hats, and their other garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace."

Dan 3:25 — "He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God."

Dan 3:27 — "And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was an hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them."

Modern Corruption

The narrative is preached as a promise that faith secures rescue, which quietly deletes the three men’s own but if not — the clause that makes their stand worth anything.

expand to see more

The corruption is the deliverance-guaranteed reading. Daniel 3 is a favourite text for teaching that God will rescue those who stand firm, and the furnace is presented as proof that faithfulness is always vindicated in this life. The three Hebrews themselves refuse that theology in the moment of testing. Our God whom we serve is able to deliver us — and then, without pause, but if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. They stated in advance that their obedience did not depend on being spared. Strip that clause out and the story becomes a transaction: stand firm and you will be rescued. Leave it in, and it becomes a doctrine of God worth dying for.

Recover the plain sense: the God who delivered these three did not deliver James from Herod’s sword, and the same chapter of Hebrews that tells of those who quenched the violence of fire tells also of those who were sawn asunder and of whom the world was not worthy. Both are faith. What Daniel 3 does prove is that the Lord is with His people in the fire — a fourth figure walking loose in the flames — and that what burns is the bindings. Nebuchadnezzar saw men loose, which they had not been when they went in. Sometimes the fire is how God unties a man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon hosa, leg-coverings — the old plural; itemised entering the furnace so the miracle could be verified leaving it.

expand to see more

Hosen — old plural of hose; Saxon hosa, a leg-covering.

Formed as oxen from ox; the modern plural is hose.

Dan 3:21 lists the garments going in; Dan 3:27 checks them coming out.

Not a hair singed, not a coat changed, not the smell of fire upon them.

Dan 3:25: they went in bound and were seen walking loose.
